scope: Finite protocol models; implementation refinement and whole-backend coverage remain incomplete.

assumptions: One organization and reservation, integer money units, balance 5, hold 1..3, actual cost 0..8.
A transition abstracts a committed database transaction; failures before commit roll back.
Does not prove numeric rounding, SQL isolation, provider outcomes, or TypeScript refinement.
Four rows in a total timestamp/ID order, two initially fail, and the run budget can visit all four.
The cursor advances after every selected row and resets for the next cron invocation.
Does not prove progress under an unbounded backlog, continuous insertion, or unfair scheduling.
Intended contract only; implementation conformance is pending private review.
Two concurrent callers, two tenants, bounded clock, and atomic decision/receipt commit.
Proof validity abstracts cryptographic checks; no cryptographic or implementation proof is claimed.
One agent projection; initialize, stop and publication acknowledge independently.
Failures may repeat forever; no availability or eventual recovery assumption.
Capacity, actual runtime cleanup and cross-agent effects require implementation tests.
Two server owners and one agent; compare-and-delete is atomic.
Status writes may fail between Redis and Kubernetes; reconcile and watch writes serialize per server.
Does not prove Redis availability, Kubernetes watch delivery, or eventual convergence.
Single controller per server name. Same-name pod/incarnation ownership and process-restart fencing are excluded.
Two installed grants of two units, two immutable request IDs, maximum reservation 1..3, costs 0..3, clock 0..4.
Transactions are atomic; request identifiers and cancellation capabilities are unique.
Provider execution, grant minting/refill, SQL reconciliation and implementation refinement are excluded.
One task, two writers and tenants, versions 1..6, clock 0..4, three history elements and two import fingerprints.
CAS retries, expiry and deletion, owner filtering and pre-serving idempotent import are modeled.
Arbitrary unconditional replacement, the Redis backend, semantic task status transitions and implementation refinement are excluded.
A foreign read closes the abstract import phase, conservatively earlier than implementation; this restricts import interleavings.
History is set-valued in this model; ordering, multiplicity, and byte fidelity are not proved.
One manager serializes snapshots, local retirement and close. Redis writes and ownership-checked cleanup acknowledge separately.
Replacement ownership appears only after local release; live cross-server stale writers, Redis expiry, actor generations and process crashes are outside this model.
Does not establish TypeScript refinement or unbounded progress.
One absolute deadline and three ordered shutdown phases; each operation may acknowledge, reject or stall.
The bounded clock abstracts elapsed monotonic scheduling; a disconnected terminal state denotes failed teardown, not proof that runtime effects completed.
No fairness, operating-system process termination or cleanup of remote provider effects is proved.
One payment, two provider events, two workers, eight clock ticks, bounded attempts.
The final lease check and transport start form one abstract action; arbitrary process suspension between those operations is excluded.
Late in-flight and duplicate deliveries are allowed. No receiver-side exactly-once, HMAC, SSRF or database/network atomicity proof is claimed.
One immutable command and scope, two workers, three lease generations, nine clock ticks, two subscription revisions.
Only committed database actions are modeled; interrupted transactions stutter.
Provider payload validation, decimal arithmetic, external idempotency and special cancellation/import authority are excluded.
Two transactions contend for one organization and one attempt in a consistent row-lock order.
Models row-lock acquisition and release only; money, provider effects, triggers, fairness and unbounded database executions are excluded.
One logical container, two row incarnations, one restart, one newer deployment, placement metadata A-to-B-to-A and one bookkeeping update.
The original created_at database text identifies a row; malicious reuse of both its UUID and exact timestamp is excluded.

Migration0558 advances the canonical lifecycle revision for all typed Hetzner placement fields; funded restart advances it even when already deploying. Full metadata equality alone does not prove absence of ABA.
Database CAS is atomic. Provider health truth, physical node replacement outside retained identity, transport reliability, liveness and TypeScript refinement are not proved.
One tenant projection, two app generations/row incarnations, one metadata change and atomic publication CAS.
Original database timestamp text identifies the row; privileged reuse of both UUID and exact timestamp is excluded. Publication retains original tenant/app generation across provider I/O.
Retirement and publication serialize at the database write. Stale cleanup can release only the original row/generation slot.
Provider truth, physical node reincarnation, later ingress publication, unbounded liveness and TypeScript refinement remain unproved.
Job-lease revocation without a changed app generation is outside this model. The separate provisioning-execution model and runtime gate do not establish model composition.
One durable job, two execution generations and a clock bounded to six ticks. The same app generation may survive job recovery.
Job, lease and dependent-resource locks serialize a committed write; lease time is rechecked after the resource lock. No TypeScript or SQL isolation refinement is proved.
Provider dispatch and completion remain external. A lease timeout or cancellation does not prove remote quiescence; an explicit witness retains overlapping old and new provider calls.
No fairness, eventual completion, provider-side fencing, or cross-job routing ownership is proved.
One organization, immutable two-unit credit quote, one Session and PaymentIntent, two provider create calls and two refund amounts.
Transactions and receipt publication are atomic. Provider idempotency is assumed within the original retained window; the separate clock model does not establish compositional refinement.
Cryptography, arbitrary decimals, SQL isolation, unbounded provider/network delay and TypeScript refinement are not proved.
Independent database and application clocks each range over 0, 22, 44 and 66 hours; up to three create attempts.
Only primary database time authorizes a new dispatch. The first dispatch time is immutable; audit updates do not restart the retry window.
This is a bounded time-gate model, not a proof of provider key retention, network arrival time, remote exactly-once behavior or implementation refinement.
Two fixed line grammars, chunks of one to three atoms, and explicit EOF or abort.
Atoms abstract complete JSON payloads; this checks segmentation and terminal behavior, not arbitrary JSON, UTF-8 decoding, provider usage, billing or TypeScript refinement.
Runtime tests separately exercise full payload bytes, Unicode, CRLF, usage receipts and cancellation.
Two observer attempts, one kernel flock, one heartbeat thread per owner, one persisted history bit.
All persistent writers run in one process. Graceful shutdown joins the heartbeat before releasing the lock; process death ends every thread before kernel release.
Scheduling fairness, exact metric bytes, disk failures, GPU readiness and Python refinement are not proved.
One fixed terminal restore and immutable S0 attempt, one counted slot, two concurrent trusted coordinator turns and two node occurrences.
One-shot Docker creation may finish after lease expiry and tombstone. Exact ID or producer quiescence is required before proof.
Database settlement is atomic. Provider receipt validity, SSH authentication, cryptographic digests and immutable source authority are assumptions exercised separately by integration tests.
The original operation never leaves failed_terminal; unavailable node or daemon proof retains quarantine. No liveness, arbitrary backlog fairness or TypeScript refinement is proved.
Three fixed terminal operations, page size two, and two completed cycles; two operations lack proof permanently and the third can settle.
Row locks select distinct operations and the database clock places selected operations after existing unselected work before remote I/O.
No unbounded backlog, new arrivals, worker availability, general liveness or implementation refinement is proved.

One original wallet/network, two durable outboxes, chain nonces zero through two, one unrelated pending transaction and one configured-wallet rotation. Signed bytes and transaction identity remain immutable; activity from the replacement wallet is outside this model.
Signing and persistence commit atomically under the wallet lock. One matching successful chain receipt is trusted as nonce consumption; arbitrary reorgs, RPC dishonesty and cryptography are excluded.

Account deletion preserves unconfirmed signed authority. Terminal recovery observes the original receipt without another send. The model does not establish TypeScript/SQL refinement, safe retry of reverted sweeps, or liveness.

A matching original receipt remains recoverable after configuration rotation. Any new send still requires current-wallet authorization; disabled networks and unbounded external configuration changes are not modeled.
Two PostgreSQL transactions, one payment and one sweep outbox. Receipt publication and deletion take the payment lock before its child outbox lock.

Deletion retains unconfirmed signed authority. Transaction completion or rollback releases both row locks. A matching receipt is already available; provider receipt validity is covered by the nonce model.
The model checks this finite lock order and includes the reversed-order deadlock witness. It does not establish fairness, database implementation refinement or freedom from unrelated lock cycles.
Three callers and physical reads; generation and revision range over 0..2. Credential startup and queued credential writes have settled before modeled read allocation.
A revision change prevents joining an older read. Existing callers may still receive an older revision; only generation fences returned data.

The model checks shared-read identity, conditional finalizer cleanup and account-generation rejection. Native gateway and provider response classification are exercised by the conformance hook, not proved by this model.
Provider state can change within one network round trip. No network fairness, permission freshness beyond that window, JavaScript refinement or external-system liveness is proved.

A shared 20-second AbortSignal deadline covers fetch and body parsing. Its callback must be scheduled and the transport must honor abort; timeout settles as unavailable, never as authorization success. Timer fairness and wall-clock delivery are not proved.
One request, two owner identities, epochs 0..2; inference and owner reads acknowledge independently.
Matches source admission timing: requestEpoch is captured after inference readiness. A reset during inference discards the memo and reads current ownership again.
Dispatch and reply separately recheck current ownership. Upstream conversation-ID allocation, credential-provider truth, task presentation, streaming and process shutdown are outside this model.
One retained Cloud encoder slot, two encoding kinds, three asynchronous loads and two callers.
Each caller retains its own load promise. Replacing the cached encoding does not replace an existing caller's result; failure clears only the matching cache entry.

Timer cancellation and callbacks follow a single JavaScript event loop. Rank-module contents, exact BPE output and idle-release behavior are checked by the real implementation conformance hook. The hook also checks the real API-server import graph.

The OpenAI per-encoding persistent cache is regression-tested by the hook but is not represented by the one-slot model. No GC reclamation deadline, network/scheduler fairness or TypeScript refinement is proved.
One stale key and at most three sequential background loaders; delivery expiry, loader completion, cache publication and ownership release are separate events.
A delivery timeout cannot cancel the loader. Permanently hung uncancellable work retains its key and consumes one queue slot; no eventual recovery or provider-success guarantee is claimed.
Cold misses and cache-read failures join a retained background result. Cold-only loads keep their existing non-coalesced policy and are outside the finite single-owner property.
Loaders must not recursively await a cold read of the same owned key. In-tree SWR callers delegate to leaf database queries or provider catalog reads.

Cache writes succeed atomically in the model; real local Redis regression separately delays a write. Cross-process ownership, invalidation races, backend outages and elapsed wall time remain unproved.

The default conformance hook uses real HTTP and the production MemoryCacheAdapter with a 100 ms test deadline. Optional CACHE_SWR_TEST_REDIS_BINARY and CACHE_SWR_TEST_REAL_DEADLINE=1 run local Redis and the production 30 second timeout.
Five keys and capacity four. Inserting a new key at capacity evicts the oldest key to the existing 75 percent target before insertion.
Entries do not expire during this trace. Reads and replacements promote recency; replacement preserves all other keys.
TTL expiry, wall-clock changes, payload aliasing, prefix matching and caller authorization are outside this finite model.

Real implementation regressions also exercise replacement at the shared-agent resolver production capacity of 1,000 entries and its 15,000 ms TTL, without claiming full-route latency or authorization proof.
One durable job, two execution generations, two retries, database clock0..6, application and database timezone offsets -2/0/2, and a two-tick delay/lease.
Committed job and lease writes are atomic. Original generation, owner and snapshot/payload fences remain required; decoded millisecond timestamps alone are not ABA authority.
Raw claim timestamps use the same column decoder as typed reads. Job timestamp-without-timezone comparison values are bound as UTC text; database-local SQL clock expressions own relative schedules.
Renewal waits may outlive their transaction-start lease. The new expiry is sampled after acquiring the job row; another generation cannot be overwritten.

No scheduler fairness, eventual execution, provider quiescence, unbounded clock behavior, DST transition semantics or TypeScript/SQL refinement is proved. Real PostgreSQL tests separately cover process and database timezone matrices and lock waits.
Two namespaces and one old session plus one already-admitted preparation. The real binding switch retains the old namespace but does not route old session IDs to it.

The target namespace must first exist through operator host-only provisioning; missing target blocks activation. The release gate checks live admission freeze, exact source/namespace identity and decision-time attestation expiry twice. Drain is human-trusted evidence, not measured by the gate. The proved step assumes that claim is true, includes all in-flight preparations, and admission remains quiesced until the switch; excluded false-claim and thaw witnesses violate safety.

Provider closure and terminal accounting are separate abstract acknowledgements. Namespace retention and receipt ordering do not prove eventual retirement, Cloudflare propagation, rollout readiness, live latency or TypeScript refinement. Real Workerd tests demonstrate the old-session routing boundary; metadata and shell tests exercise the release gate.
